### Data

I aggregated buffer data by their spatial clustering because otherwise there would be pseudoreplications due to closely spaced points. This meant averaging calculated continuity statistics for Guezen and Forrest's data by the "site" identity since their points were transects that were closely spaced (within ~ 1km) inside site groups. Aaron's data had "farm" groupings but these didn't always mean they were closely spaced. Instead, I grouped points that were 1km within each other and averaged them. Hemberger and Williams's sites were selected to be more than 1km apart so I didn't have to do this for their data. Instead of averaging, I could also have randomly selected one point in each group and used that to calculate continuity statistics, but I think the results will be similar.

The aggregation process resulted in 149 total points (27 Guezen & Forrest, 35 Hemberger & Williams, and 87 Iverson). The % natural area vs crop shannon diversity is shown below.

```{r}

ggplot(all.mn, aes(pct.natural, crop.shandiv, color = study)) +
  geom_point() + scale_shape_manual(values = c(12,8,1)) +
  scale_color_discrete() + egg::theme_article()

```

I'm focusing on three statistics summarizing temporal change in floral resources:

- The **mean** floral resources across time points
- The **coefficient of variation** across time points - I've switched back to CV because the behavior of "stability" (1/CV) seems funny to me. As differences between time points approach perfect equality, CV gets smaller, so the stability value approaches infinity. This results in a heavy emphasis on sites where floral resources almost didn't change at all, which creates outliers.
- The **scaled peak time** represents the weighted mean flowering time on a unit scale that represents the entire "season" of each study. To calculate, I took the average of the time points weighted by their flower counts and then scaled by the number of timepoints used in the study, so max flowering time across all studies was one. This is a method that performed well in a comparison of peak flowring estimates by [Taylor (2019)](http://dx.doi.org/10.7717/peerj.7720).
- For Aaron's data, I used the 5-timepoint subset.

For each of the stats I fit generalized linear models with % natural area and crop shannon diversity as predictors. I used likelihood ratio tests to compare models with linear relationships to quadratic ones, and with interactions.

## Mean floral resources over the season

### Plots

```{r}
#| fig-cap: Percent natural area against mean floral resources over time. Floral resource means have been z-scaled based on their associated study's distribution. Points are colored by location shannon diversity and shape is study.

ggplot(all.mn, aes(pct.natural, flr.mn.zscale, color = crop.shandiv, shape = study)) +
  geom_point() + scale_shape_manual(values = c(12,8,1)) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(option = "turbo", direction = -1)

```


```{r}
#| fig-cap: Crop shannon diversity against mean floral resources over time. Floral resource means have been z-scaled based on their associated study's distribution. Points are colored by location % natural area and shape is study.

ggplot(all.mn, aes(crop.shandiv, flr.mn.zscale, color = pct.natural, shape = study)) +
  geom_point() + scale_shape_manual(values = c(12,8,1)) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(option = "mako", direction = -1)

```

### Model comparisons

I use a gamma family GLM because floral resource means are non-negative. I also fit a dispersion parameter that varies by study, since the plots suggest that each study's values are differently dispersed.

```{r}
library(glmmTMB)
library(lmerTest)
library(DHARMa)

glm.flrmn1 <- glmmTMB(flr.mn ~ crop.shandiv + pct.natural + study, 
                      dispformula = ~ study,
                      family = Gamma(link = "log"),
                      data = all.mn)

glm.flrmn2a <- glmmTMB(flr.mn ~ crop.shandiv + poly(pct.natural,2) + study, 
                      dispformula = ~ study,
                      family = Gamma(link = "log"),
                      data = all.mn)

glm.flrmn2b <- glmmTMB(flr.mn ~ poly(crop.shandiv,2) + pct.natural + study, 
                      dispformula = ~ study,
                      family = Gamma(link = "log"),
                      data = all.mn)

glm.flrmn3 <- glmmTMB(flr.mn ~ crop.shandiv *pct.natural + study, 
                      dispformula = ~ study,
                      family = Gamma(link = "log"),
                      data = all.mn)

glm.flrmn4a <- glmmTMB(flr.mn ~ crop.shandiv + poly(pct.natural,2) * study, 
                      dispformula = ~ study,
                      family = Gamma(link = "log"),
                      data = all.mn)

glm.flrmn4b <- glmmTMB(flr.mn ~ (crop.shandiv + poly(pct.natural,2)) * study, 
                      dispformula = ~ study,
                      family = Gamma(link = "log"),
                      data = all.mn)

glm.flrmn4c <- glmmTMB(flr.mn ~ (poly(crop.shandiv,2) + poly(pct.natural,2)) * study, 
                      dispformula = ~ study,
                      family = Gamma(link = "log"),
                      data = all.mn)

# glm.flrmn4a <- glmmTMB(flr.mn ~ crop.shandiv * poly(pct.natural,2) + study, 
#                       dispformula = ~ study,
#                       family = Gamma(link = "log"),
#                       data = all.mn)
# 
# glm.flrmn4b <- glmmTMB(flr.mn ~ poly(crop.shandiv,2) * pct.natural + study, 
#                       dispformula = ~ study,
#                       family = Gamma(link = "log"),
#                       data = all.mn)
# 
# glm.flrmn4c <- glmmTMB(flr.mn ~ poly(crop.shandiv,2) * poly(pct.natural,2) + study, 
#                       dispformula = ~ study,
#                       family = Gamma(link = "log"),
#                       data = all.mn)



```

Likelihood ratio tests comparing linear model to quadratic % natural area or quadratic crop shannon diversity. Quadratic natural area term is supported, while quadratic crop shannon diversity is not.

```{r}

anova(glm.flrmn1, glm.flrmn2a)
anova(glm.flrmn1, glm.flrmn2b)

```

Likelihood ratio tests comparing linear model linear interaction model. The interaction model isn't supported.

```{r}

anova(glm.flrmn1, glm.flrmn3)

```

Study interactions are supported for both percent natural area and with crop shannon diversity, but doesn't change (lack of) support for a quadratic crop shannon diversity effect.

```{r}

anova(glm.flrmn2a, glm.flrmn4a, glm.flrmn4b, glm.flrmn4c)

```

### Selected model coefficients

This is a look at some of the models from the comparisons above.

**Fitted model coefficients.** Crop shannon diversity is significant in the all linear models but is not significant when a quadratic term for % natural area is added.

## Coefficient of variance

### Plots

```{r}
#| fig-cap: Percent natural area against coefficient of variance of floral resources over time. Points are colored by crop shannon diversity and shape is study.

ggplot(all.mn, aes(pct.natural, flr.cv, color = crop.shandiv, shape = study)) +
  geom_point() + scale_shape_manual(values = c(12,8,1)) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(option = "turbo", direction = -1)

```

```{r}
#| fig-cap: Crop shannon diversity against coefficient of variance of floral resources over time. Points are colored by percent natural area and shape is study.

ggplot(all.mn, aes(crop.shandiv, flr.cv, color = pct.natural, shape = study)) +
  geom_point() + scale_shape_manual(values = c(12,8,1)) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(option = "mako", direction = -1)

```

### Model comparisons

I fit gaussian distribution regression models. I also fit a dispersion parameter that varies by study.

```{r}

glm.flrcv1 <- glmmTMB(flr.cv ~ crop.shandiv + pct.natural + study, 
                      dispformula = ~ study,
                      data = all.mn)

glm.flrcv2a <- glmmTMB(flr.cv ~ crop.shandiv + poly(pct.natural,2) + study, 
                      dispformula = ~ study,
                      data = all.mn)

glm.flrcv2b <- glmmTMB(flr.cv ~ poly(crop.shandiv,2) + pct.natural + study, 
                      dispformula = ~ study,
                      data = all.mn)

glm.flrcv3 <- glmmTMB(flr.cv ~ crop.shandiv * pct.natural + study, 
                      dispformula = ~ study,
                      data = all.mn)

glm.flrcv4a <- glmmTMB(flr.cv ~ crop.shandiv + poly(pct.natural,2) * study, 
                      dispformula = ~ study,
                      data = all.mn)

glm.flrcv4b <- glmmTMB(flr.cv ~ (crop.shandiv + poly(pct.natural,2)) * study, 
                      dispformula = ~ study,
                      data = all.mn)


```

Likelihood ratio tests comparing linear model to quadratic % natural area or quadratic crop shannon diversity. Quadratic natural area term is supported, while quadratic crop shannon diversity is not.

```{r}

anova(glm.flrcv1, glm.flrcv2a)

anova(glm.flrcv1, glm.flrcv2b)

```

Likelihood ratio tests comparing linear model linear interaction model. The interaction model is supported over the no-interaction model, but AIC and BIC are not as good as the quadratic % natural area model.

```{r}

anova(glm.flrcv1, glm.flrcv3)

```

Likelihood ratio tests support an interaction between (quadratic) natural area terms and study. Interaction between study and crop shannon diversity is not supported.

```{r}

anova(glm.flrcv2a, glm.flrcv4a, glm.flrcv4b)


```

## Peak flowering time

### Plots

```{r}
#| fig-cap: Percent natural area against scaled peak flowering time. Points are colored by location shannon diversity and shape is study.

ggplot(all.mn, aes(pct.natural, pktime.scale, color = crop.shandiv, shape = study)) +
  geom_point() + scale_shape_manual(values = c(12,8,1)) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(option = "turbo", direction = -1)

```

```{r}
#| fig-cap: Crop shannon diversity against scaled peak flowering time. Points are colored by location % natural area and shape is study.

ggplot(all.mn, aes(crop.shandiv, pktime.scale, color = pct.natural, shape = study)) +
  geom_point() + scale_shape_manual(values = c(12,8,1)) +
  scale_color_viridis_c(option = "mako", direction = -1)

```

### Model comparisons

I use a gamma regression to model peak flowering time. I also fit a dispersion parameter that varies by study.

```{r}

glm.pktime1 <- glmmTMB(pktime.scale ~ crop.shandiv + pct.natural + study, 
                       family = Gamma(link = "log"),
                       dispformula = ~ study,
                       data = all.mn)

glm.pktime2a <- glmmTMB(pktime.scale ~ crop.shandiv + poly(pct.natural,2) + study, 
                        family = Gamma(link = "log"),
                       # family = beta_family(),
                       dispformula = ~ study,
                       data = all.mn)

glm.pktime2b <- glmmTMB(pktime.scale ~ poly(crop.shandiv,2) + pct.natural + study, 
                        family = Gamma(link = "log"),
                       # family = beta_family(),
                       dispformula = ~ study,
                       data = all.mn)


glm.pktime2bx <- glmmTMB(pktime.scale ~ poly(crop.shandiv,2) * study + pct.natural, 
                        family = Gamma(link = "log"),
                       # family = beta_family(),
                       dispformula = ~ study,
                       data = all.mn)

glm.pktime2c <- glmmTMB(pktime.scale ~ crop.shandiv + poly(pct.natural,2) * study, 
                        family = Gamma(link = "log"),
                       # family = beta_family(),
                       dispformula = ~ study,
                       data = all.mn)

glm.pktime2d <- glmmTMB(pktime.scale ~ (crop.shandiv + poly(pct.natural,2)) * study, 
                        family = Gamma(link = "log"),
                       # family = beta_family(),
                       dispformula = ~ study,
                       data = all.mn)


glm.pktime2e <- glmmTMB(pktime.scale ~ (poly(crop.shandiv, 2) + poly(pct.natural,2)) * study, 
                        family = Gamma(link = "log"),
                       # family = beta_family(),
                       dispformula = ~ study,
                       data = all.mn)

glm.pktime3 <- glmmTMB(pktime.scale ~ crop.shandiv * pct.natural + study, 
                       family = Gamma(link = "log"),
                       # family = beta_family(),
                       dispformula = ~ study,
                       data = all.mn)

glm.pktime3a <- glmmTMB(pktime.scale ~ crop.shandiv * poly(pct.natural,2) + study,
                        family = Gamma(link = "log"),
                       # family = beta_family(),
                       dispformula = ~ study,
                       data = all.mn)

glm.pktime3b <- glmmTMB(pktime.scale ~ poly(crop.shandiv,2) * pct.natural + study,
                        family = Gamma(link = "log"),
                       # family = beta_family(),
                       dispformula = ~ study,
                       data = all.mn)

glm.pktime3c <- glmmTMB(pktime.scale ~ crop.shandiv * pct.natural * study,
                        family = Gamma(link = "log"),
                       # family = beta_family(),
                       dispformula = ~ study,
                       data = all.mn)

glm.pktime4a <- glmmTMB(pktime.scale ~ poly(crop.shandiv,2) * poly(pct.natural,2) + study,
                       family = Gamma(link = "log"),
                       # family = beta_family(),
                       dispformula = ~ study,
                       data = all.mn)


```

Likelihood ratio tests comparing linear model to quadratic % natural area or quadratic crop shannon diversity. Both quadratic terms are supported.

```{r}

anova(glm.pktime1, glm.pktime2a, glm.pktime2c, glm.pktime2d, glm.pktime2e)
anova(glm.pktime1, glm.pktime2b, glm.pktime2bx, glm.pktime2e)

anova(glm.pktime2bx, glm.pktime2d)

```

Interaction term is also supported.

```{r}

anova(glm.pktime1, glm.pktime3)

```

Interacting quadratic percent natural area and crop shannon diversity is also supported, but not the best AIC/BIC

```{r}

anova(glm.pktime3, glm.pktime3a, glm.pktime4a)
anova(glm.pktime3, glm.pktime3b, glm.pktime4a)

```

#### Interaction model coefficients

Adding an interaction makes everything significant.

```{r}

sjPlot::tab_model(glm.pktime3)

```

:::{.callout-note collapse="true"}
##### Interaction model diagnostics

```{r}

glm.sim <- DHARMa::simulateResiduals(glm.pktime3)

plot(glm.sim)

plotResiduals(glm.sim, all.mn$pct.natural)
plotResiduals(glm.sim, all.mn$crop.shandiv)
plotResiduals(glm.sim, all.mn$study)

performance::check_model(glm.pktime3)

```

:::

#### Interaction of quadratic percent natural area and crop shannon diversity model coefficients

Adding interacting quadratic % natural terms are significant.

```{r}

sjPlot::tab_model(glm.pktime2d)

```

:::{.callout-note collapse="true"}
##### Quadratic % natural and studyinteraction model diagnostics

```{r}

glm.sim <- DHARMa::simulateResiduals(glm.pktime2d)

plot(glm.sim)

plotResiduals(glm.sim, all.mn$pct.natural)
plotResiduals(glm.sim, all.mn$crop.shandiv)
plotResiduals(glm.sim, all.mn$study)

performance::check_model(glm.pktime2d)

```

:::




## Land cover floral density comparisons

We can also make a comparison between crop and % natural area land covers. I haven't done this yet, but based on the patterns in the following plots, it seems like the trends are that natural land covers have more floral resources on average, while having lower CV (more continuous). Crop land covers have a later peak time.

```{r}
#| fig-cap: Mean floral resources comparison by land cover group and study.

ggplot(lcflrcv, aes(crop, flr.mn.scale, fill=crop)) + 
  geom_jitter(aes(color = crop)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha=0.3) + facet_wrap(~study)

```

```{r}
#| fig-cap: Coefficient of variation in floral resources over time by land cover group and study.

ggplot(lcflrcv, aes(crop, flr.cv, fill=crop)) + 
  geom_jitter(aes(color = crop)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha=0.3) + facet_wrap(~study)

```


```{r}
#| fig-cap: Scaled time of peak floral resources by land cover group and study.

ggplot(lcflrcv, aes(crop, pktime.scale, fill=crop)) + 
  geom_jitter(aes(color = crop)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha=0.3) + facet_wrap(~study)

```
